CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain retaliatory posture with the recently announced tariff increases on $60B of US goods, activate the unreliable entity list framework, and prepare rare-earth export controls as a contingency — but avoid full-scale escalation. Leave the door open for G20 talks in late June while demonstrating China will not capitulate under pressure.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is severe but not yet existential (threat_score: +0.6). Three factors drive this reading: (1) The Huawei Entity List designation (May 16) strikes directly at China's technology ambitions — Google suspended Android access and US chip suppliers paused sales, threatening Huawei's global smartphone and 5G equipment businesses, which are central to Made in China 2025. (2) Manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in May with new export orders at 46.5 and employment at 47.0 (lowest since March 2009), confirming the tariff war is already biting China's real economy. (3) Trump has directed preparation of 25% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese imports, which would cover virtually all bilateral trade — the OECD projects this could reduce Chinese GDP by over 1.1%. However, China retains meaningful countermeasures (rare earths, unreliable entity list, fiscal stimulus capacity) and services PMI remains in expansion at 54.3, preventing a reading at the existential end.

The action stance (action_score: -0.3, retaliate) reflects the strategic calculus that China must signal resolve without overextending. Retaliation is justified because: (a) China's June 1 tariff increases on $60B of US goods and the unreliable entity list announcement demonstrate China will not accept unilateral pressure, which is essential for domestic legitimacy and negotiating leverage; (b) the rare-earth threat, while experts call it 'loud saber-rattling' (Business Insider, June 2), has already prompted the Pentagon to seek new funding for domestic US production — the signal alone has strategic value; (c) with the G20 Trump-Xi meeting expected in late June, maintaining retaliatory pressure preserves negotiating cards. But full escalation is inadvisable because: the weak PMI and employment data show China's economy cannot absorb unlimited shocks; rare-earth weaponization would accelerate US/ally diversification (as happened after the 2010 Japan incident); and former PBOC governor Dai Xianglong has already signaled low expectations for a G20 breakthrough, suggesting patience is the wiser course.
key_factors: Huawei Entity List (May 16) — existential threat to China's tech champion and 5G ambitions
Manufacturing PMI at 49.4, export orders at 46.5, employment at 47.0 — trade war biting real economy
US preparing 25% tariffs on remaining ~$300B of Chinese imports
China's rare-earth leverage (80% market share) — effective as signal but risky to fully weaponize
G20 Trump-Xi meeting expected late June — opportunity window for de-escalation
Unreliable entity list announced May 31 — new retaliatory tool available
OECD projects 1.1% GDP hit to China in worst-case escalation scenario

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.

May's figure was 49.4, the first time the manufacturing PMI has slipped into negative territory since February... The employment sub-index dropped from 47.2 to 47.0, the lowest reading since March 2009.
If tariffs expand to cover all U.S.-China trade... Chinese GDP would be 0.8% lower. Scenario with equity shock: 0.9% lower.
China's threat to withhold rare-earth materials from the US is most likely just a form of 'loud saber-rattling' to get the US to return to negotiations.
Under worst-case scenario for escalation... Chinese GDP would likely be more than 1.1% lower.
